RagShortTexts: A ram needs repeated impacts, a usable approach, a sound frame and a coordinated crew.
Missiles, ditches and gate construction delay ramming; timber and cover also matter.

Variants.Content: At a Rus wooden town or Baltic stronghold, a ram must first cross ditches, slopes and obstacles. A carried beam and a heavier suspended one require different approaches and crews. Each stroke needs recovery. A roof gives some protection from missiles but adds weight, while defenders can use hooks, fire and stones to obstruct movement.

A ram crew needs coordinated effort and attention to the frame and ground. Sunken wheels or a shifted support can waste the force of the men behind. Relief crews, shields and removal of debris matter; wounded men also need an exit from the crowded approach.

A commander must compare the time and provisions required for an approach, ditch work and cover. Assigning every carpenter to a ram reduces wagon and camp repairs. Sustained use needs relief crews. If the gate is exposed to flanking fire, improving cover and access matters more than repeated attempts without cover.

A siege ram consumes long timbers, ropes, vehicles and transport, often demanded from nearby communities. Carriers need an unloading place and a route home, while animals left behind must still work fields. A prolonged siege increases lost labor and food costs for carpenters, drivers and farmers together.
